title: The Soviet Lead
description: Why both superpowers ended up funding parapsychology in the 1950s

concepts.title: Vasiliev and Soviet Bioinformation
concepts.contentHtml:
From the 1920s the USSR ran modest state-funded experiments on telepathy and 'bioinformation transfer' — figures like Leonid Vasiliev at Leningrad University tested mental influence at a distance, sometimes inside Faraday cages to rule out radio.

Stalin's purges suppressed parapsychology in the 1940s. It re-emerged after Khrushchev's 1956 thaw, with new institutions in Leningrad and Novosibirsk. By the 1960s, Western intelligence assessed (with limited evidence but high concern) that the Soviets were spending tens of millions of roubles annually on psi research with possible military applications.

concepts.title: The 1970 Inflection Point
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1970 book Psychic Discoveries Behind the Iron Curtain by Sheila Ostrander and Lynn Schroeder reported (often credulously) on Soviet parapsychology, and was widely read inside US intelligence. Combined with rumours of a Soviet submarine-comms experiment using telepathy (the so-called Nautilus experiment, almost certainly a hoax), this triggered a 'psi gap' panic.

The CIA's logic: if the Soviets believed in this, and if it might work even slightly, the US could not afford not to investigate. A small budget was set aside. The actual scientific case was thin from the start.

concepts.title: The Strategic Frame
concepts.contentHtml:
Cold War psi programs were never primarily about science — they were about strategic-uncertainty management. If a hostile state was running parapsychology programs, the cost of being wrong (the enemy actually had a working psi capability) was catastrophic. The cost of being right (parapsychology doesn't work) was modest research dollars.

This calculus produces decades of well-funded work on hypotheses with weak evidence. It also produces strong institutional incentives to find positive results — researchers' careers depend on programs continuing, and reviewers within the agency tend to be less hostile than scientific peer review.

Both effects are visible in the historical record.

concepts.title: Origins
concepts.contentHtml:
MK-Ultra began in 1953 under CIA Director Allen Dulles. Its mandate was to investigate techniques for behavioural modification — drugs, hypnosis, sensory deprivation, electroshock, biological agents — with applications in interrogation, induced amnesia, and behavioural conditioning of foreign agents.

The catalyst was the Korean War: returning American POWs had given confessions that US officials interpreted as 'brainwashing' (the term was Edward Hunter's 1950 coinage). Whether the Chinese had actually developed mind-control techniques was unclear; whether the US should have a counter-capability was, to MK-Ultra's planners, obvious.

concepts.title: Subprojects and Drugs
concepts.contentHtml:
MK-Ultra ran 149 subprojects at universities, hospitals, prisons, and military bases — most via cut-out funding through front foundations to avoid CIA attribution. Subjects often did not consent or know they were being tested. LSD was a primary tool: dosed onto agents, contractors, and unwitting members of the public, sometimes in 'safe houses' with one-way mirrors.

Notable consequences: in 1953 biochemist Frank Olson was secretly dosed with LSD at a CIA retreat. Days later, distressed and possibly psychotic, he fell from a 13th-floor New York hotel window. The death was ruled suicide; later investigations and a 1994 forensic examination raised serious questions about whether he was pushed.

concepts.title: The Cover-up and Disclosure
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1973, CIA Director Richard Helms ordered all MK-Ultra files destroyed. The destruction was incomplete: financial records survived in a separate archive. In 1975 the Church Committee in the US Senate and the parallel Rockefeller Commission revealed MK-Ultra's outline to the public. Subsequent FOIA releases and the 1977 Senate hearings filled in details.

What's confirmed: the program existed, ran for 20 years, dosed unwitting subjects with drugs, contributed to at least one death (Olson), and produced no operational mind-control capability. Whether the Chinese 'brainwashing' it was meant to counter ever existed in a meaningful technical sense remains debated. The Korean POW confessions are now generally explained by ordinary coercion, sleep deprivation, and isolation — not exotic technique.

concepts.title: Origins at SRI
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 1972 the CIA contracted Stanford Research Institute (SRI), specifically physicists Russell Targ and Hal Puthoff, to investigate parapsychological claims under controlled conditions. The work focused on remote viewing: a subject in one location attempts to describe a target location they have not been told about.

Initial subjects included artist Ingo Swann, who claimed psychic abilities. Targ and Puthoff developed a protocol where viewers attempted to describe target sites visited by 'beacon' team members; descriptions were judged for accuracy by independent rankers.

concepts.title: The Pat Price Hits and Misses
concepts.contentHtml:
Several reportedly striking cases came out of SRI: Pat Price, a former police commissioner, allegedly described a Soviet research site at Semipalatinsk in the 1970s with details that startled briefers. Other Price hits and high-profile claimed successes (a downed Soviet Tu-22 located, a kidnapped Italian general's location identified) became internal-CIA folklore.

On methodological re-examination, many of these are less impressive than they first appear: feedback loops where viewers received cues, post-hoc selection of best-matching descriptions, and judges who were not blinded to the program's interest in positive results. The successes are real in the sense that they happened — but their statistical significance, controlled for these issues, is much weaker than the lore suggests.

concepts.title: Joe McMoneagle and the Long Run
concepts.contentHtml:
The program transferred from CIA to Army intelligence (DIA) in the late 1970s and was renamed several times — Grill Flame, Center Lane, Sun Streak — before being collected as Stargate in 1991. By 1995 the cumulative budget had reached approximately $20 million.

Joe McMoneagle, an army warrant officer turned full-time remote viewer, was the most successful and longest-tenured 'operational' viewer. McMoneagle and others worked on real intelligence tasks: locating downed aircraft, profiling foreign sites, sometimes attempting to describe hostage locations. The DIA's internal assessment of operational value was mixed and frequently contested.

title: The 1995 AIR Review
description: How the program was finally killed

concepts.title: The Review
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1995 the CIA, transferred Stargate's evaluation to the American Institutes for Research (AIR), which commissioned two reviewers: statistician Jessica Utts (sympathetic to the parapsychology hypothesis) and psychologist Ray Hyman (skeptical).

Their reports diverged sharply. Utts argued that the laboratory data showed statistically significant effects above chance, suggesting a real phenomenon. Hyman argued that the same data, examined for methodological flaws, did not robustly support the existence of psi — and that operational utility was negligible.

concepts.title: The Decision
concepts.contentHtml:
The CIA agreed with Hyman's assessment of operational utility regardless of the lab statistics question. Whatever psi was producing in carefully-controlled SRI experiments, it was not producing actionable intelligence in the real world. Stargate was cancelled in 1995 and most files were declassified.

The declassified record is now publicly available. It shows: a long history of laboratory work with mixed statistical results; a small set of striking-sounding operational stories that mostly fail close methodological re-examination; and a very large amount of routine, unsuccessful, and embarrassing work that doesn't appear in popularised accounts.

concepts.title: What Statistics Can and Can't Show
concepts.contentHtml:
Utts' technical case is more interesting than skeptics often grant. The aggregated SRI data does, by standard statistical tests, show effects significantly above chance. That doesn't automatically mean psi: it means either (a) psi exists, or (b) some methodological flaw is producing apparent effects across many studies — for example, sensory cueing, judging bias, or selective reporting.

Hyman's position is the standard scientific one: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and 'small effects above chance, hard to replicate elsewhere' is not extraordinary. As of 2026 no replication of SRI-style remote-viewing protocols outside the original group has produced robust effects.

The phenomenon, if it exists, is small and difficult to elicit. The practical question — whether to invest in it — is different from the existence question and was answered no.

title: What This Tells Us
description: Programs, incentives, and the cost of strategic uncertainty

concepts.title: Why Strategic-Uncertainty Programs Survive
concepts.contentHtml:
Programs justified by 'we can't afford to be wrong about the enemy capability' have a structural advantage: they continue as long as the enemy might have the capability, regardless of whether your own results are positive.

Both MK-Ultra and Stargate ran for over 20 years on weak scientific evidence because the strategic frame demanded continued investigation. Once the Cold War ended, the strategic frame relaxed and the programs were closed promptly — Stargate in 1995, several similar projects elsewhere in the same window.

concepts.title: Why Insider Reviews Find What Outsider Reviews Don't
concepts.contentHtml:
The pattern across MK-Ultra, Stargate, and similar programs: insider reviews tend to find positive results, often citing operational successes that outsider methodologists later discount. Why?

Selection bias on cases (only striking cases are reviewed). Researchers' careers depend on programs continuing. Insider reviewers share strategic frame: 'even small positive results justify continuation.' Outsider reviewers apply standard scientific criteria and find the work falls short. The asymmetry is structural, not malicious.

The lesson generalises: when a program's existence depends on its own findings, expect findings to support continuation. This is true for parapsychology, for several drug-development programs, and for many policy-research programs in any era.

concepts.title: What's Genuinely Confirmed
concepts.contentHtml:
Confirmed by declassified record: MK-Ultra dosed unwitting subjects with drugs; Frank Olson died in unclear circumstances after being dosed; Stargate ran for over two decades with $20M+ in cumulative funding; remote-viewing protocols produced statistically positive aggregate results in laboratory conditions; operational utility was concluded to be negligible.

Not confirmed: that mind-control techniques were achieved, that remote viewing produced repeatable practical intelligence, that any significant Cold War operation was meaningfully shaped by psi-program output. The closer you look at specific success stories, the thinner they become.

Both programs are real history. Their findings, taken at face value, are mostly cautionary tales about institutional incentive structures rather than evidence of paranormal capabilities.
